label: Baseline
description: What is the starting point for AI and innovation skills?
body:
Foundational work in AI and labor economics shows that skill distribution at baseline determines both the pace and the equity of technology adoption. Our baseline data is allowing us to map public servants’ starting points across core competencies, identify where skill gaps are largest, and differentiate between individual-level limitations (e.g., unfamiliarity with prompting) and structural barriers (e.g., policy restrictions).

Understanding the starting point allows us to understand the impact of training and upskilling. Our pre-training surveys include items measuring self-reported AI knowledge levels, confidence in applying AI skills, and familiarity with specific AI competencies across multiple courses including Using GenAI at Work, Scaling AI, and domain-specific programs.

label: Tasks
description: What tasks are public servants already performing with AI?
body: Studies across industry show that the benefits of AI depend heavily on task design—which tasks are automated, augmented, or transformed. By documenting what public servants do with AI (summarizing documents, generating drafts, coding, data cleaning, citizen communication, etc.), we can identify emerging patterns of productivity and risk. Our surveys ask respondents to identify specific tasks they perform with AI, including creating text, analyzing data, writing code, brainstorming, conducting research, and synthesizing information, through items in our pre- and post-course instruments.

label: Challenges
description: What obstacles do workers face when using AI?
body: The literature shows that organizational frictions—unclear policies, lack of access, inconsistent guidance—are often bigger barriers than skill deficits. Our open-ended data allows us to surface insights into these real-world constraints, giving leaders insight into where governance, not technical training, is the bottleneck. We collect data on barriers through items asking why respondents are not using AI (e.g., uncertainty about permissions, lack of knowledge, limited access) and through open-ended feedback questions across our course evaluations and workshop surveys.

label: Risk
description: What unsafe or noncompliant behaviors occur before training?
body: Before formal training, workers often engage in insecure practices similar to those documented in private companies (e.g., pasting sensitive data into public tools). Understanding this baseline risk environment is critical for designing responsible-use programs and safeguarding public data. Our pre-course surveys ask respondents how often they engage in specific behaviors when using AI, including inputting sensitive data, checking outputs against other sources, looking for bias, and disclosing AI use to others.

label: Variation
description: How do adoption patterns differ across roles, agencies, and geographies?
body: The literature shows that adoption varies by occupation, managerial responsibility, and access to tools. Our demographic and occupational data allow us to identify which groups adopt fastest and where additional support is most needed. Our surveys collect demographic information including government level (federal, state, county, municipal), years in government, managerial status, work function, age, gender, and race/ethnicity, allowing us to analyze patterns across different workforce groups.

label: Judgment
description: How do workers evaluate the accuracy and risks of AI-generated content?
body: Human oversight is essential for safe AI use. Our data begins to illuminate how public servants gauge the reliability of AI output, an area heavily studied in journalism, software development, and academia but underexplored in government. Survey items ask how often respondents check AI outputs against other sources and look for bias in AI-generated content, providing initial insight into responsible use.

label: Modalities
description: Which training formats produce the strongest learning outcomes?
body: The education and workforce training literature shows that the type and style of training matter. By comparing asynchronous courses and workshops, we may gain insight into which formats yield the strongest, most durable gains for different types of learners. We deliver training through both self-paced asynchronous courses and facilitated multi-session workshops, each with distinct survey instruments, enabling comparison of outcomes across delivery formats.

label: Persistence
description: Do workers sustain and apply what they learn?
body: Longitudinal research indicates that without reinforcement, new digital skills degrade over time. Our 3–6 month follow-up surveys evaluate whether learning persists, transforms workflows, and diffuses across teams—the elements associated with durable organizational change. We want to understand if and how training translates into long-term behavior change.

label: Effectiveness
description: How do improved skills affect government performance?
body: Private sector data link AI literacy to gains in speed, accuracy, and service quality. We capture self-reported workflow improvements—faster case processing, better communication, improved analysis—that can later be paired with organizational metrics to demonstrate performance impact in government. Post-course surveys and 6-month follow-ups collect open-ended examples of accomplishments and applications, along with ratings of course value and likelihood of applying learned skills, providing self-reported indicators of workflow improvement.

label: Gains
description: Does training measurably increase skills, confidence, and responsible use?
body: Private-sector studies repeatedly show that structured training increases productivity and decreases error rates. Our pre/post training assessments allow us to assess these effects in the public sector across technical proficiency, ethical reasoning, and domain-specific application. We administer matched pre- and post-course assessments measuring knowledge, confidence, and skill application across our programs, with Likert scale items on topics such as prompt-writing ability, responsible use confidence, and domain-specific competencies.

label: Attitudes
description: How does learning shift perceptions—from risk to value?
body: AI adoption research consistently shows that mindset shift is a precursor to behavior change. Our data track how training changes attitudes such as reducing fear, increasing confidence, and heightening perceived usefulness. Here, multiple survey items capture attitudes toward AI, including whether respondents believe AI will make their work easier or harder, how likely they think AI will change their day-to-day tasks, and their confidence in using AI responsibly, measured both before and after training.
